item.title: The Complexity of Choosing Parity Projections
item.description: arXiv:2611.00289v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cube attacks in cryptanalysis seek small sets of Boolean variables (cubes) whose parity sum is constant. We study the bounded constant derivative problem introduced by Smirnov (2026), which seeks a smallest cube with sum 1, and its sum-0 analogue. Despite their similarity, the problems differ sharply in parameterized complexity: the sum-1 problem admits a $2^{O(k^2)}\operatorname{poly}(N)$-time algorithm, where $k$ is cube size, whereas the sum-0 problem is not fixed-parameter tractable unless $\mathrm{FPT}=\mathrm{W}[1]$. Without a bound on cube size, both problems are $\Sigma_2^{\oplus\mathrm{P}}$-complete and NP-hard to approximate within $N^{1-\varepsilon}$ for every fixed $0<\varepsilon<1$. Our hardness proofs use a crown construction that embeds maximal monomials of parity-projected circuits into positive 2CNF. This yields completeness and inapproximability results, as well as a dichotomy for Boolean constraint languages of arity at most two: the bounded constant derivative problem is in P when all relations are affine and $\Sigma_2^{\oplus\mathrm{P}}$-complete otherwise. We also give algorithms parameterized by the number of quadratic rounds, treewidth, or ordered branching-program width, with lower bounds for the first two unless $\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{SUBEXP}$. The treewidth lower bound holds for circuits; the case of 2CNF remains open.
item.dc:creator: Karthik Sheshadri, Nicholas Smirnov

item.title: Limits and Constants of OpenAI's Claimed ETH Refutation
item.description: arXiv:2611.00517v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A recent OpenAI preprint claims a deterministic algorithm that counts the satisfying assignments of a $k$-CNF formula in time $2^{O_k(n\log\log n/\sqrt{\log n})}$, and $2^{O(n/\sqrt{\log n})}$ at bounded clause density, which would refute the Exponential Time Hypothesis. The headline bound is proved by tensor contraction; the body develops an interpolation algorithm with the weaker exponent $n(\log\log n)^2/\sqrt{\log n}$. This note does four things. First, it explains the interpolation algorithm in plain terms. Second, it asks how large $n$ must be for the bounds to bite. The preprint states no constants, so we treat the hidden constant $C$ as a parameter: the general bound beats the $2^n$ of brute force only beyond $n\approx 10^{32}$ for $C=2$, $10^{126}$ for $C=3$ and $10^{3517}$ for $C=10$. We then extract the constants from the tensor-contraction proof: for every input with $m$ clauses at bounded density, the running time it certifies stays above $2^n$ unless $\log_2(n+m)>10^9$, and on random 3-CNF at the satisfiability threshold unless $\log_2 n>5\times10^{11}$. So the bounds are subexponential as $n\to\infty$, but the proof certifies no speed-up over brute force for any input of bounded density that could ever be written down. Third, for the clause-product form of the interpolation algorithm we prove limits in a cost model matching the preprint's evaluation. By a short algebraic lemma, polynomial cost needs components of $O(\log^3 n)$ variables with per-point evaluation, or primal treewidth $O(\log^2 n)$ with dynamic programming over the groups. So the scheme costs $2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\mathrm{tw}})}$ at treewidth $\mathrm{tw}$, $2^{\Omega(\sqrt n)}$ with high probability on random 3-CNF above clause density 3, and $2^{\Omega(n^{1/3})}$ even on trivially countable path formulas. We explain why the preprint's sharper routes escape these limits. Fourth, we report experiments.
item.dc:creator: Fabio Dias, Yvens Lima

item.title: On the complexity of isomorphism problems for tensors, groups, and polynomials V: over commutative rings
item.description: arXiv:2611.00735v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tensors over commutative rings naturally appear in number theory, geometry, and group theory. For example, $2\times 2\times 2$ tensors over $\mathbb{Z}$ form the starting point of Bhargava's celebrated works generalising Gauss's composition law (Bhargava, Ann. Math., 2004). Symmetric tensors over $\mathbb{Z}$ are central to the classification of Calabi--Yau threefolds (Yau, Commun. Pure Appl. Math., 1978; Wall, Invent. Math., 1966), geometric objects of significance in string theory. Additionally, tensors over finite commutative rings closely correspond to finite nilpotent groups of class 2 (Baer, Trans. Am. Math. Soc., 1938). In this work, we study isomorphism testing of tensors over commutative rings from a complexity-theoretic viewpoint, and its applications. Some of our main results are: 1. Let $\mathrm{R}$ be a commutative ring. We introduce two complexity classes: $\mathsf{3TI}_\mathrm{R}$ consisting of problems that are polynomial-time reducible to isomorphism problems of tensor products of three modules over $\mathrm{R}$, and $\mathsf{3FTI}_\mathrm{R}$ consisting of problems that are polynomial-time reducible to isomorphism problems of tensor products of three free modules over $\mathrm{R}$. 2. We show that some classical problems considered by Grunewald and Segal (ibid.), and the problem of classifying Calabi--Yau threefolds, are $\mathsf{3FTI}_\mathbb{Z}$-complete. We also show that many natural problems are complete for $\mathsf{3TI}_{\mathbb{Z}/p^e\mathbb{Z}}$. 3. We show that testing isomorphism of tensors in $\mathbb{Z}^2\otimes\mathbb{Z}^2\otimes\mathbb{Z}^2$ is polynomial-time equivalent to the principal ideal problem in algorithmic number theory. 4. We present an $N^{O((\log N)^{8/9})}$-time algorithm for testing isomorphism of finite nilpotent groups of class $2$ and odd order $N$.
item.dc:creator: Joshua A. Grochow, Youming Qiao, Katherine E. Stange, Xiaorui Sun

item.title: Approximate clearing in financial networks with credit default swaps: hardness thresholds, a box algorithm, barriers, and exact solvency at bounded degree
item.description: arXiv:2611.00855v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study approximate clearing in financial networks with credit default swaps. For weak notions (W) and (I), we prove PPAD-hardness below a threshold approximately $0.2530$ and give a polynomial-time interval algorithm above a threshold approximately $0.2834$. On networks whose CDS writers are solvent ex ante, the corresponding bounds are $(13-\sqrt{153})/4$ and $3-2\sqrt{2}$, approximately $0.1577$ and $0.1716$. The thresholds are sharp for bounded-radius algorithms: for (I) on writer-solvent networks, and for (I) and (W) in general. On non-degenerate networks, (W) and (I) have identical hardness and tractability threshold endpoints. For exact-solvency notion (D), PPAD-hardness holds at every rational error $\varepsilon<1$ on non-degenerate networks. On a restricted unit-notional class, let $d$ be the maximum number of CDS contracts held by a core bank, counted with multiplicity. For rational $\varepsilon\in[1/2,1)$, writing $\rho=(1+\varepsilon)/(1-\varepsilon)$, the problem is polynomial-time solvable when $d<(\lceil\rho\rceil+1)\rho$ and PPAD-complete otherwise. At $\varepsilon=1/3$ the boundary is $d=5$ versus $d=6$; below $\varepsilon=1/9$, degree $2$ is already PPAD-complete, while degree $1$ is exactly solvable. These degree results concern (D) and do not close the (W)/(I) approximation windows. We also establish a barrier to Pure-Circuit reductions certified by interval propagation under stated interface and auxiliary-bank restrictions. A finite-precision interval algorithm reduces writer-solvent (I) to point selection in near-stalled boxes; selection is polynomial-time when the residual matrix is symmetric or monotone on each strongly connected component. The general and writer-solvent approximation windows remain open.
item.dc:creator: Michal \v{C}ert\'ik

item.title: Nonnegative Rank Bounds for the Algebraic Monotone Calculus
item.description: arXiv:2611.01055v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In Hrubes' Algebraic Monotone Calculus a DNF tautology $A$ is proved by a monotone arithmetic circuit computing $\chi(A)-\epsilon\chi(1)$ for some $\epsilon>0$, where the coefficient of $\chi(A)$ at $x^\sigma$ counts the terms of $A$ satisfied by $\sigma$, and $\chi(1)=\prod_i(x_i^0+x_i^1)$. Proof size is circuit size, and $\epsilon$ is existentially quantified, so lower bounds must hold at arbitrarily small $\epsilon$. We prove lower bounds for bounded-depth fragments by two nonnegative rank measures of the target: monotone tensor rank and the nonnegative rank of a flattening. At depth three a proof is a nonnegative tensor decomposition. Restricting its terms to subcube indicators gives conical juntas, a system polynomially equivalent to Sherali-Adams in twin variables. For arbitrary terms we adapt Rothvoss' hyperplane separation to monotone tensor rank: Tseitin formulas on constant-degree expanders of large girth need proofs of size $2^{\Omega(\epsilon n)}$ whenever $\epsilon=\omega(\log n/n)$. This cannot reach every $\epsilon$: at shift $2^{-\Theta(n\log n)}$ Tseitin acquires polynomial-size depth-three proofs, separating the two fragments exponentially. A constant-size index gadget gives bounds for every $\epsilon\geq2^{-\Omega(n)}$, converting a Sherali-Adams degree bound into a size bound. Depth three is essential: Tseitin has monotone proofs of size $O(n^3)$ and depth $O(\log n)$ at every $\epsilon$. Beyond depth three we bound the nonnegative rank of a flattening by $L^{2^t}$ for a monotone formula with $L$ leaves and mixed-product depth $t$: the largest number of product gates on a root-to-leaf path whose two inputs each meet both sides of the bipartition. Approximate extension complexity then bounds perfect matching and odd factor instances, and planted CSP integrality gaps give an explicit family of planted Tseitin DNFs hard at inverse-polynomial shift.
item.dc:creator: Fedor Part

item.title: A Numerical Refinement of an Exact Discrete Fourier Transform Bound
item.description: arXiv:2611.01257v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We refine the numerical bounds in Kartal's instantiation of Sussman's exact discrete Fourier transform construction. For every integer n >= 1, the resulting algorithm computes the length-n transform with work O(n (log n)^(1 - delta)), where delta = 0.0030201659. The bound holds in an exact complex-arithmetic RAM model with a supplied canonical root of unity. This final exponent saving exceeds the earlier certified parameter C_0 = 0.00302016 by 5.9 x 10^(-9). We retain the underlying circuit, tighten rational bounds for sums of powers of its block and target ranks, and increase the fixed tensor power from 7760 to 11640. These bounds establish the inequalities for Sussman's recursion at the intermediate certificate parameter C = 0.00302016595. The gap C - delta absorbs the overhead of recursion and Fourier reduction. The resulting transform theorem is proved in Lean and checked against the reference problem statement.
item.dc:creator: Zhihao Yao, Sichao Liu

item.title: A Decomposition Theorem and a Simple Algorithm for Contraction Fixed Points
item.description: arXiv:2611.01302v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove a decomposition theorem for the problem of computing an approximate fixed point of a contraction map $f\colon [0,1]^k \to [0,1]^k$ under the $\ell_{\infty}$-norm. After a preliminary version of the decomposition theorem appeared on arXiv [CLY26], Feodorov and Haslebacher [FH26] gave a striking application of the theorem, showing that it can be used to convert any $\operatorname{poly}(k,\log(1/\varepsilon))$-query algorithm with running time $(k\log(1/\varepsilon))^{O(k)}$ into an algorithm with running time $(k\log(1/\varepsilon))^{O(\sqrt{k})}$. They instantiated this framework with an $O(k^2\log(1/\varepsilon))$-query algorithm with the desired running time, thereby obtaining the first subexponential-time algorithm for contraction fixed points under the $\ell_{\infty}$-norm and, via well-known reductions, the first deterministic subexponential-time algorithm for simple stochastic games and mean-payoff games. In addition to the decomposition theorem, as our second main result in this paper, we show that the $O(k\log(1/\varepsilon))$-query algorithm of [CLY25] can be implemented in time $(k\log(1/\varepsilon))^{O(k)}$; our algorithm may be viewed as conceptually simpler compared to the algorithm of [FH26]. A key observation here is that the function constructed in [CLY25], whose fixed points are used as the next query points, turns out to be nonexpansive under the $\ell_{\infty}$-norm, so the brute-force procedure can be replaced by known algorithms for contraction fixed points.
item.dc:creator: Xi Chen, Yuhao Li, Mihalis Yannakakis

item.title: The Exact Communication Threshold for Parallel Repetition
item.description: arXiv:2611.01339v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The parallel repetition theorem is a fundamental tool in theoretical computer science, showing that the probability of winning all $n$ independent instances of a finite two-player game decays exponentially in $n$, provided that the game has no perfect strategy. The classical theorem assumes that the players cannot communicate, raising the question of how much communication can be allowed while preserving this exponential decay. For every finite total relation $g$ and arbitrary input distribution $\mu$, we prove exponential decay at every fixed communication rate below a quantity called zero-error internal information complexity, denoted by $\mathrm{IC}_{\mu}(g,0)$. Together with known results showing that $n\,\mathrm{IC}_{\mu}(g,0)+o(n)$ bits of communication suffice to solve all $n$ instances with success probability tending to one, our bound determines the exact communication threshold. As a by-product, we obtain exact characterizations of amortized distributional and randomized communication complexity under the global-error criterion.
item.dc:creator: Daiki Suruga

item.title: Improved NP-Hardness of Approximation for Max-3-Cut and for Max-k-Cut with Small k
item.description: arXiv:2611.01402v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that Max-3-Cut is NP-hard to approximate within a factor of $27/29+\varepsilon \approx 0.931$. This improves the factor $16/17 \approx 0.941$ of Austrin, O'Donnell, Tan and Wright, the best NP-hardness result for Max-3-Cut since 2012. (Their result, unlike ours, also holds for 3-colourable graphs.) We also improve the NP-hardness of Max-$k$-Cut for every $k$ from 4 to 20; for instance, we obtain $45/47 \approx 0.957$ for Max-4-Cut and $33/34 \approx 0.971$ for Max-5-Cut, where the previous factors were 0.987 and 120/121. Our reductions are gadget reductions from H{\aa}stad's linear equations over $\mathbb{Z}_3$, with gadgets that have at most six auxiliary vertices. The main new idea is a negation trick: since the negation of an assignment is again an assignment, equations with right-hand sides $t$ and $-t$ can be handled together, and this makes the resulting predicates symmetric under all permutations of the colours. We complement it with a general soundness criterion for such reductions: in effect, the best strategy of the adversary is to use a single colour pattern everywhere. This criterion is the strongest analysis that uses H{\aa}stad's theorem as a black box, and, using LP duality, we show that under it no gadget reduction from these equations can beat $27/29$ for Max-3-Cut. Finally, we observe that a classical reduction from Max-3-Cut to Max-$k$-Cut, applied more carefully, already gives $82/85 \approx 0.965$ for Max-4-Cut on 4-colourable graphs, improving the previously stated $85/86$.
item.dc:creator: Ziang Ni

item.title: The Runtime-Moment Frontier for Universal Sampling
item.description: arXiv:2611.01884v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can one sampler give every string at least a polynomial fraction of the probability that any source in a class gives it, while keeping a bounded moment of its own runtime? We answer this in terms of runtime moments. For every oracle and every rational $a>0$, one sampler with polynomial $a$th runtime moment dominates every source with polynomial $r$th moment with power $B(a,r)=1+(a-\min\{r,1\})_+/r$, and the R\'enyi divergence of order $B/(B-1)$ of the source from it is $O(\log n)$, a sharp quantitative form of Gurevich's domination on average. Relative to an oracle, $B(a,r)$ is optimal in both senses, with failures at every large input length. So the first moment is a threshold: one sampler of order one is universal for expected polynomial time, but none of higher order is universal even for polynomial-space sources with all polynomial moments. For expected-polynomial-time sources the threshold also holds relative to a random oracle and, without an oracle, under a sequential-hardness hypothesis on iterated functions or a parallel-sequentiality hypothesis on verifiable delay functions with short seeds. The frontier governs algorithms as well. For rational orders we determine the exact exponent by which polynomial runtime moments of deterministic deciders transfer from one fixed sampler to every source, and show, relative to oracles, that all correct solvers of a sparse language in $\mathsf{UP}\cap\mathsf{coUP}$ meet it. Where $B(a,r)=1$, actual running times transfer better than arbitrary costs, but only above a critical moment.
item.dc:creator: Sebastian Ben Daniel

item.title: Factor Closure in Noncommutative Algebraic Complexity
item.description: arXiv:2611.02039v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that $\VPnc$ is closed under taking factors over every field. If a noncommutative circuit of size $s$ computes a nonconstant polynomial of degree at most $D$, then each left or right factor has a circuit of size $O(sD^3)$. A central factor $g$ in a decomposition $f=agb$, with nonconstant outer factors $a,b$, has a circuit of size $O(sD^6)$. The proof uses a small weighted nondeterministic finite automaton (NFA) with replacement labels. Given $f=gh$, its labels depend on a word of maximum degree in $h$ and the coefficients of its suffixes. A pairing of accepting paths proves that the induced linear map $T$ satisfies $T(gh)=g$. Matrix substitution implements $T$ in a circuit. Applying the same substitution to a Boolean-sum verifier proves $\VNPnc$ closure. The construction also proves formula closure. The automaton has one copying state and, after leaving it, uses only scalar replacements. This structure gives formulas of size $O(s^2)$ for one-sided factors and $O(s^4)$ for central factors of a size-$s$ formula. The same map proves that polynomial-size noncommutative algebraic branching programs are closed under taking factors. Polynomial-size ABP factorizations over finite fields are already known from~\cite{AJ25}. These are arithmetic size bounds, with arbitrary field constants at unit cost, including over $\Q$. Over finite fields, combining the formula construction with~\cite{AJ22} gives randomized polynomial-time complete factorization of formula inputs, with factors output as formulas. For polynomial-degree circuit inputs, we obtain polynomial-length succinct ABP descriptions with polynomial-time edge queries. We also give two algorithms that output complete ordered irreducible factorizations as polynomial-size circuits: a deterministic $\FP^{\SigTwo}$ algorithm and a zero-error randomized algorithm with an NP oracle and expected polynomial running time.
item.dc:creator: V. Arvind, Pushkar S. Joglekar

item.title: Pointwise Score Evaluation from Succinct Boolean Descriptions: SAT Equivalence for Strongly Log-Concave Gaussian Mixtures
item.description: arXiv:2611.02346v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Score-based generative models rely on access to accurate scores, but the cost of computing those scores depends on how the underlying distribution is represented. Can smoothness and strong log-concavity make score evaluation efficient when a distribution is specified by Boolean constraints? I investigate this question by separating geometric encoding from computational extraction. I construct a succinctly specified Gaussian mixture whose score at a fixed query location encodes whether a Boolean formula is satisfiable. The construction has rational component means and uniform strong log-concavity, yet deterministic polynomial-time approximation of the designated score coordinate to constant absolute accuracy is equivalent to polynomial-time solvability of Boolean satisfiability. This equivalence remains valid throughout a neighborhood whose radius is independent of dimension. I further characterize how numerical precision connects bounded witness enumeration to exact counting, and show that independent sample access turns the same target into a dimension-independent mean-estimation problem. An explicit parity construction also separates low-degree approximation from efficient computation. Together, these results show that favorable geometry alone does not resolve the computational cost of extracting scores from compact descriptions. They identify the precise extraction requirement in this formulation while leaving the existence of a general efficient evaluator open.
item.dc:creator: Yinzhen Lv

item.title: Exponential Lower Bounds for Products of Cubic Polynomials over Prime Fields
item.description: arXiv:2611.02385v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study exact representations of explicit signed modular predicates on $\{-1,1\}^n$ as products of bounded-degree polynomials over prime fields, measured by total variable-occurrence cost. Our main result is an exponential lower bound for products of cubic polynomials. Over $\mathbb F_3$ the proof is self-contained: every cubic factor in a nonvanishing product is a unit on the sign cube, the unit identity forces bounded affine-observation complexity, and a simultaneous clustering argument converts this structural compression into an exponential occurrence lower bound. We also give an alternative reconstruction route that isolates the quadratic structure behind the cubic classification. We then extend the cubic theorem to every fixed prime field $\mathbb F_p$ of characteristic greater than three for odd target modulus $q$ coprime to $p$. The only non-elementary structural input in this extension is Karam's restricted-range rank theorem; the conversion from multiplication to parity and the $p$-tuple clustering argument are proved explicitly. Finally, we establish a coefficient-field-independent degree-lifting principle. If a lower bound is known at one fixed degree, restriction to a large independent set yields a quantitative lower bound at the next degree. In particular, the exponential cubic theorem implies $ L^{(p,q)}_4(n)=\Omega_{p,q}\!\left(\frac{n^4}{(\log(2+n))^3}\right). $ For the characteristic-three core this already gives a lower bound for a restricted mixed-modulus circuit class.
item.dc:creator: Bin Fu, Yunhui Fu

item.title: ETH is Dead, Long Live SH
item.description: arXiv:2611.02650v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Impagliazzo and Paturi's 1999 Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH) is false, but Stearns and Hunt's 1990 Satisfiability Hypothesis (SH) remains plausible. We prove that SH is equivalent to the recently proposed Weak ETH which rules out $O(2^{n^{1-\varepsilon}})L^{O(1)}$-time 3SAT algorithms for every constant $\varepsilon>0$, where $L$ is the input length. We show that SH (or Weak ETH) preserves the typical process for lower bounds: a polynomial-time reduction from a 3SAT formula of size $s=\Theta(n+m)$ to an instance of size $N\le s^{b+o(1)}$, for fixed blowup exponent $b>0$, rules out $O(2^{N^{1/b-\varepsilon}})$-time algorithms for every constant $\varepsilon>0$. By comparison, for an $N=O(s^b)$ blowup, ETH would have ruled out $2^{o(N^{1/b})}$-time algorithms. The framework also yields parameterized lower bounds ruling out running times of the form $O(2^{k^{1/b-\varepsilon}})L^{O(1)}$. We also prove equivalence of the analogous counting hypotheses, #SH and Weak #ETH, and that they rule out $O(2^{(n+m)^{1-\varepsilon}})$-time algorithms for #2SAT for every constant $\varepsilon>0$.
item.dc:creator: MIT Hardness Group, Josh Brunner, Erik D. Demaine, Fabian Frei, Timothy Gomez, Markus Hecher, Jeffery Li, Jayson Lynch

item.title: Fine-Grained Complexity Across the Computational Phase Transition
item.description: arXiv:2611.02702v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How does a computational problem transition from easy to hard? In the hard-core model, approximate counting and sampling are polynomial-time tractable up to tree uniqueness, but worst-case intractable at any constant relative distance above it unless $\mathsf{NP}=\mathsf{RP}$. We quantify the transition from polynomial to exponential mixing for classical Glauber dynamics. On $n$-vertex graphs of maximum degree $d\ge3$, at fugacity $\lambda=(1+\delta)\lambda_{\mathrm c}(d)$ with sufficiently small $\delta\ge0$ that may vanish with $n$, its worst-case mixing time has the form $\exp\{\Theta(n\delta^2/d)\}n^{1+\Theta(1)}$. The upper bound is degree-uniform, and the matching lower bound holds for every fixed $d$. Annealing gives approximate counting with the same running-time upper bound at fixed accuracy. For general sampling and counting algorithms, we establish a robust fine-grained reduction from SAT without assuming a lower bound on SAT's running time. For any fixed $d\ge3$ and $0<\gamma<1$, a sampling or approximate-counting algorithm running in $\exp\{O((n\delta^2/d)^{1-\gamma})\}\operatorname{poly}(n)$ time along any one suitable inverse-polynomial distance sequence $\delta=\delta(n)$, yields a randomized SAT algorithm running in $\exp\{\widetilde O(s^{1-\gamma})\}$ time on inputs of binary length $s$. This power-saving transfer identifies $n\delta^2/d$ as the analogue of SAT input length for hard-core sampling and counting at relative distance $\delta$ above criticality: beating the Glauber exponent by a fixed power through any sampling or counting method would yield a corresponding power improvement for SAT. At criticality, we establish $O(\sqrt{n/d})$ spectral independence, optimal in $n$ at fixed degree, and degree-uniform Glauber mixing in $\widetilde O(n(n/d)^{1+1/(d-2)})$ time, improving the previous $\widetilde O(n^{4+4/(d-2)})$ bound.
item.dc:creator: Zhe Ju, Jingcheng Liu, Yitong Yin

item.title: Exact Agreement Expansion up to the Top via Non-polarity
item.description: arXiv:2611.03261v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agreement expansion asks whether local assignments to faces of a poset that usually agree on a sampled common face must agree with a single global function on most faces. Agreement expansion is exact (approximate) if local assignments need to exactly (approximately) agree with the global function. We suggest a new proof technique for agreement expansion that enables agreement expansion in settings which were previously beyond reach, such as: exact agreement expansion for Grassmannian posets (before only simplicial complexes support exact agreement expansion); agreement expansion based on assignments to top faces of the a complex (before agreement expansion is generally proven only for assignments to low dimensional faces); agreement expansion from one-sided spectral expansion (before, two sided spectral assumption was needed in general settings). Specifically, for down-closed simplicial and Grassmannian complexes, we prove an exact agreement theorem between any two layers assuming one-sided spectral expansion in links of singletons. As an application, we show that full bases of every rank-$k$ matroid admit exact agreement with soundness $O(k^2/[h(k-h)])$ when tested through $h$-element independent sets. We also obtain exact agreement on Grassmannian posets under one-sided spectral expansion, with stronger soundness under a local distance guarantee. Our key proof ideas center around non-polarity of the distributions of local assignments, probed via a random exposure of elements.
item.dc:creator: Tali Kaufman, Huy Tuan Pham

item.title: Online Algorithms Cannot Find Isolated Perceptron Solutions
item.description: arXiv:2611.03397v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The binary perceptron problem asks for a length-$n$ sign vector in the intersection of $\lfloor \alpha n\rfloor$-many independent random Gaussian half-spaces. A striking feature of this model is strong freezing: at every constraint density $\alpha > 0$, all but a vanishing fraction of solutions are isolated -- $\Omega(n)$-far from all others, in Hamming distance. Such solutions are believed to be algorithmically inaccessible. Nevertheless, efficient algorithms find solutions at some constraint densities $\alpha$. One possible resolution of this apparent contradiction is that the solution space also contains rare well-connected structures, and that algorithms succeed by locating them. Gong, Huang, Li and Sellke (FOCS 2026) proved this for stable algorithms, by showing that such algorithms cannot locate isolated solutions with probability more than $\approx 0.84$. In this work, we study online algorithms, which receive the columns of the constraint matrix one by one and sign each irrevocably upon arrival. This is a widely used class of algorithms in discrepancy minimization, and it includes the algorithm of Jo and Lee (2026), which has one of the best provable guarantees for the binary perceptron. We prove that at any constraint density, any online algorithm outputs an isolated solution with probability $o(1)$. Our proof is based on the observation that the signs an online algorithm has already fixed can be completed to at most one isolated solution, so a successful algorithm must choose the unique correct sign for each of the last few columns. Using the exchangeability of these columns, we show that such an algorithm must match a suffix-parallel baseline, which signs each of them as if it were the next column to arrive. We then use an anti-concentration argument to show that such a baseline rarely produces a unique completion.
item.dc:creator: Shuangping Li, Gabe Schoenbach

item.title: Parity Decision Trees of Depth $O(4^d \log\|\widehat f\|_1)$ for Boolean Functions $f$ of $F_2$-Degree $d$
item.description: arXiv:2611.03452v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let $f\colon F_2^n\to\{-1,+1\}$ have $F_2$-degree $d\ge2$. We prove that its deterministic parity decision tree depth satisfies \[ D_{\oplus} (f)= O(4^d \log_2\|\widehat f\|_1) = O(4^d \log_2 s(f)), \] where $\|\widehat f\|_1=\sum_\xi|\widehat f(\xi)|$ is the Fourier spectral norm and $s(f)$ is the Fourier sparsity. The bound is linear in the logarithm of the spectral norm for every fixed degree, with singly exponential dependence on $d$. This improves the previously best known bound of $O(2^{d^2/2} \log^{d-2} \|\widehat f\|_1)$ due to Tsang, Wong, Xie and Zhang (FOCS 2013). Our result establishes the log-rank conjecture for $\mathrm{XOR}$ functions of $F_2$-degree $O(\log\log s(f))$, extending the previously accessible range $d=O(1)$. The proof combines field lifting, multiplicative derivatives, a multiplicity-based generic-rank comparison, a Schur-complement vanishing argument, and dimension-preserving descent to $F_2$ to lower the degree on every coset of a common subspace.
item.dc:creator: Shengyu Zhang

item.title: Determinant boundaries and gaps in determinantal complexity
item.description: arXiv:2611.03554v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Landsberg, Manivel, and Ressayre constructed determinant-boundary components whose defining forms, for odd n >= 3, are limits of n x n determinants but cannot themselves be represented by determinants of that size. Their border determinantal complexity (DC) is therefore smaller than their exact DC. We prove that the difference can grow linearly with n. For every n >= 10, we construct an explicit homogeneous form of degree n, concise in n^2 variables, whose orbit closure is a boundary component, whose border DC is n, and whose exact DC is at least 2n - 1. Thus n rows suffice when limits are allowed, whereas every exact representation requires at least 2n - 1 rows. The same bound holds for the unpadded odd-skew forms at every odd n >= 3. We also prove that every concise degree-n boundary form in n^2 variables has exact DC at least n + 2. We construct three families of pairwise distinct boundary components. Together with the traceless determinant, they give at least floor((n-1)/2) + floor(n/3) components for every n >= 3, with an additional term counted explicitly in the paper. The main lower bound follows from a general degree lemma. If an affine matrix represents an irreducible homogeneous polynomial f of degree d and has globally free rank-one cokernel over the coordinate ring of f = 0, its size is at least 2d - 1. The adjugate factors into two nonzero kernel vectors, each requiring a coordinate of degree at least d - 1. Comparing their product with the degree of a cofactor proves the bound. The lemma is sharp for individual representations, as witnessed by algebraic branching programs. Whether the exact-versus-border gap can grow superlinearly remains open.
item.dc:creator: Karthik Sheshadri

item.title: A Circuit Complexity Trichotomy For Regular Languages
item.description: arXiv:2611.03615v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish a trichotomy for the non-uniform, unbounded-fan-in circuit complexity of regular languages: the complexity of every regular language lies in exactly one of $O(1)$, $\Omega(\log n)\cap O(\log n\log\log n)$, or $\Omega(n)\cap O(n)$. Our main technical contribution is a characterization of the sublinear class in terms of algebra, word congruences, regular expressions, and logic. This class consists precisely of the regular languages computable by constant-depth circuits of size $O(\log^2 n)$, or, equivalently, by circuits of size $O(\log n\log\log n)$ and depth $O((\log\log n)^2)$. Consequently, every regular language of sublinear circuit complexity is definable in $\mathrm{FO}^2[\Sigma,<,\mathrm{mod}]$, which is contained in wire-linear $\mathbf{AC}^0$. For each of the three classes, deciding membership is $\mathbf{PSPACE}$-complete when the language is specified by a nondeterministic finite automaton. We also obtain a corresponding classification for regular languages with a neutral letter.
item.dc:creator: Stefan G\"oller, Amaldev Manuel

item.title: FIXP-Completeness in Second-Price Auctions
item.description: arXiv:2611.00543v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Computing equilibria is a fundamental algorithmic problem in game theory and economics. Although general frameworks are available for proving membership in FIXP, the class capturing exact fixed-point computation, establishing FIXP-completeness often remains challenging. We prove FIXP-completeness of exact equilibrium computation in three second-price auction models: (1). pacing with return-on-investment constraints, with multiplier cap $1+\delta$ for every fixed rational $\delta>0$ [Filos-Ratsikas, Hansen, H{\o}gh, and Hollender (2024)]; (2). budget-constrained generalized second-price sponsored shopping [Hansen, Li, and Nie (2026)]; (3). budget-constrained throttling [Liu (2026)]. These results resolve open questions on the exact complexity of automated bidding. Our technical ingredient is a FIXP-complete generalized-circuit problem using only clipped affine gates and the reciprocal $x\mapsto1/(1+\tau x)$, for any fixed positive rational $\tau$. This gate basis provides a common framework for the three auction reductions: simulating these gates in each model establishes FIXP-hardness without directly implementing multiplication or squaring.
item.dc:creator: Nobutaka Shimizu

item.title: Compressed Oracle Duality: A simple framework for knowing what quantum adversaries know
item.description: arXiv:2611.00609v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Given a quantum adversary that queries a random oracle, how do we characterize the information that they "know"? The Compressed Oracle method of Zhandry (CRYPTO 2019) is one method that records the queries that the adversary makes; this recording serves as a representation of the information that is learned. However, a significant limitation of the Compressed Oracle method is that it may continue to store information that the adversary has "forgotten." This issue is especially pertinent in the space-bounded setting, where the adversary may uncompute information to free up space, while the information may still reside in the compressed oracle. In this work, we present a simple and interpretable framework called "Compressed Oracle Duality," which extends the Compressed Oracle method for space-bounded algorithms. By applying an isometry to the memory of a quantum adversary, we obtain a pair of compressed oracles with identical marginal distributions and classical correlations which correspond to the knowledge the adversary retains. In fact, we show that the outcome of measuring the new compressed oracle database corresponds exactly to applying the pretty-good measurement on the adversary's memory. As an application of our framework for collision search, we give a simplified proof of the recent $T^2S = \Omega(N\log N)$ quantum time-space tradeoff for label-symmetric algorithms due to Magniez-Zur (arXiv:2609.10808); we also prove a stronger classical tradeoff of $TS=\Omega(N\log N)$ assuming label symmetry. The proofs under our framework do not require representation theory and instead bound the mutual information between the compressed oracle pairs. This highlights both how the label symmetry assumption bypasses known proof barriers as well as the challenges that remain in achieving unconditional quantum time-space tradeoffs.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Ding, Mark Zhandry

item.title: Leaving Quantum Bias on the Table: Pushforwards as a Path to Quantum Advantage in Constrained Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.00759v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Constrained quantum samplers often produce infeasible outputs that retain information about good feasible solutions. We develop a post-measurement framework that constructs problem-dependent classical feasibility maps from constraint-violation statistics and pushes the raw quantum sampling law forward onto the feasible set. The probability of each repaired solution is the total raw mass of its repair preimage, enlarging the successful sampling event from a target feasible set to its full repair preimage. We derive exact identities for repaired success and expected cost, and separate repair-basin geometry from sampler-dependent probability concentration. For noisy implementations, we distinguish leakage from the encoded subspace from concentration loss within it. For permutation constraints, Hungarian maximum-overlap repair provides an O(n^3) implementation, which we study on traveling-salesman problems (TSP). We derive conditional repaired-success bounds and quantify how basin aggregation reduces the absolute-transfer budget required by these bounds. Noiseless simulations show that optimal repair basins contain selectively overweighted infeasible contributors. For an n=10 TSP instance, pushforward repair recovered the optimum using approximately 10^3 shots, compared with 10^6 shots in the original CE-QAOA workflow without repair. On a 127-qubit IBM processor, using encodings of up to 100 qubits, repaired candidates match reference tours on smaller benchmarks and improve them on larger instances. These results establish concentration of quantum probability on useful repair preimages as a design principle for constrained quantum optimization.
item.dc:creator: Chinonso Onah, Stuart Hadfield, Kristel Michielsen

item.title: Mutual-visibility colouring with two colours is NP-complete for every fixed diameter
item.description: arXiv:2611.01012v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A mutual-visibility set in a graph $G$ is a set $S$ of vertices such that any two vertices of $S$ are connected by a shortest path with no internal vertex in $S$, and the mutual-visibility chromatic number $\chi_\mu(G)$ is the minimum number of mutual-visibility sets needed to partition $V(G)$. Babu, Di Stefano and Lakshmanan showed that it is NP-complete to decide whether $\chi_\mu(G)\le 2$ for graphs of diameter four. We show that the problem remains NP-complete for graphs of diameter $d$, for every fixed $d\ge2$; diameter two is the smallest diameter for which the problem is non-trivial. The proof rests on a reformulation of $\chi_\mu(G)\le 2$ for diameter-two graphs as the $2$-colourability of an associated hypergraph, and on a reduction from $2$-colourability of $3$-uniform hypergraphs without short cycles.
item.dc:creator: Siddhesh Chaubal

item.title: The Value of Steiner Hubs in Two-Hop Distance Labeling
item.description: arXiv:2611.01106v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Two-hop distance labelings were introduced in 2002 by Cohen, Halperin, Kaplan, and Zwick with hubs of two kinds: vertices of the graph, or, in their Steiner variant, arbitrary objects carrying arbitrary real values. On no family is the value of that freedom known. We determine it on $\ell_1$ products of betweenness-free metrics, those with no point between two others, a class containing every Hamming graph. The freedom is worth nothing when the factors have at most three letters, while from four letters on the largest saving is polynomial in the size of the product, attained on products of positively weighted stars. The $d$-dimensional hypercube is the two-letter case, and labeling it takes $(5/2+o(1))^d$ entries even with arbitrary hubs, matching the vertex-hub optimum of Goldberg, Razenshteyn, and Savchenko. Every lower bound here comes from one semidefinite program on a single factor, whose value $\Lambda$ never exceeds the rate that vertex hubs already achieve on the Hamming graph; where $\Lambda$ meets that ceiling, the freedom is worth nothing, and the ceiling is met exactly up to three letters.
item.dc:creator: Sichen Wang

item.title: The Movement Complexity of Sorting
item.description: arXiv:2611.01157v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The complexity of sorting is usually measured by the number of comparisons. This measure ignores the movement of the read heads between comparisons, which is a real cost on many machines. We study this cost on its own. Keys lie on a $d$-dimensional grid, two heads move over the grid and compare the keys beneath them, and the only cost is the total movement of the heads. The algorithm plans its route in $r$ rounds and sees the outcomes of each round only after running it. For every $d$ and $r$ we determine the expected movement needed to sort $n$ keys: it is $n^{\beta}$ up to polylogarithmic factors, where $\beta=1+D^{r-1}/(D^{r}-(D-1)^{r})$ and $D=2d$, falling from $n^{2}$ at $r=1$ to $n^{1+1/(2d)}$ with unlimited rounds. Our algorithm makes every round move about the same amount, and a matching lower bound holds against every algorithm.
item.dc:creator: Sichen Wang

item.title: An $\mathsf{FPRAS}$ for Mixed Volumes
item.description: arXiv:2611.01368v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We design the first fully polynomial-time randomized approximation scheme ($\mathsf{FPRAS}$) to estimate the mixed volume of $n$ arbitrary compact convex sets in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ specified by weak membership oracles. This disproves a longstanding conjecture of Gurvits (2009). $\textbf{AI Disclosure}$ The main ideas were generated entirely by GPT 6 Astra. The purpose of this paper is to provide a human-written exposition of the algorithm.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoyu Chen, Kuikui Liu

item.title: Quantum Lower Bounds for Collision Problems
item.description: arXiv:2611.01767v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We establish tight lower bounds on the adaptive and non-adaptive quantum query complexities of Promised $k$-to-one Finding on an exactly $k$-to-one input string $x\in\mathbb Z_q^n$, for every fixed $k\ge2$ and every feasible alphabet size $q\ge n/k$. The lower bounds are $\Omega_k(n^{1/2-1/(2(2^k-1))})$ for unrestricted adaptive algorithms and $\Omega_k(n^{1-1/k})$ for one-round non-adaptive algorithms. The former matches the adaptive quantum algorithm of Liu and Zhandry [LZ19], whereas the latter matches classical birthday sampling even when the parallel queries are arbitrarily entangled. We also establish the non-adaptive lower bound $\Omega_k(\sqrt{n/k})$ for $k$-to-one Testing when $q\ge n$, resolving an open question posed by Koiran, Landes, Portier, and Yao [KLPY10]. Our proofs generate the balanced input from a uniformly random permutation and use compressed permutation oracles to describe the information learned by the algorithm. The adaptive proof bounds the growth of partial collisions through successive queries. The one-round proof instead analyzes the state after the parallel queries directly, bounding the probability that the compressed database contains a full collision. In both proofs, a short verification step accounts for correct outputs that include unrecorded positions. For the decision problem, we also compare one-round states with independent and distinct output labels.
item.dc:creator: Pan Peng, Jingyu Wu

item.title: Deterministic Polynomial-Time Primality Testing with a Single Binomial Congruence
item.description: arXiv:2611.02280v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We give a deterministic polynomial-time primality test whose main verification is the congruence $(1+X)^n=1+X^n$ in $C_n[X]/(X^r-b(Y))$, where $C_n=(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})[Y]/(\Phi_r(Y))$. Two identities in the coefficient ring normalize $b$ and ensure compatibility with the main congruence. A finite-field root count and a lattice bound show that an accepted input is a prime power; elementary preprocessing excludes nontrivial perfect powers. We construct $b$ deterministically using Jacobi sums and the uniform Dedekind-zeta zero-free theorem of Cureton and Thorner, which extends OpenAI's Hecke zero-free theorem. The total bit complexity is $L^{32+o(1)}$, where $L=\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$, and verification after constructing $b$ costs $L^{6+o(1)}$. More generally, for a fixed real algebraic $1/2\le\theta<1$, a common zero-free boundary $\Re s>\theta$ for the relevant Dedekind zeta functions gives $L^{\max\{6,(1-\theta)^{-1}\}+o(1)}$. This bound reaches $L^{6+o(1)}$ at $\theta=5/6$, and hence under GRH. We state a fixed-base modification of Agrawal's conjecture for odd integers passing the base-$2$ Fermat test, using the modulus $X^r-2$ with $r$ the least positive integer not dividing $n(n-1)$.
item.dc:creator: Joseph M. Shunia

item.title: Efficient Proper Agnostic Learning of Halfspaces
item.description: arXiv:2611.02344v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We give a proper membership-query algorithm for agnostically learning halfspaces under the uniform distribution on $\{\pm1\}^n$. Given query access to an arbitrary function $f:\{\pm1\}^n \to \{\pm1\}$, our algorithm runs in time $\mathrm{poly}(n)+2^{\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)}$ and outputs a halfspace with error at most $\mathrm{OPT}+\varepsilon$, where $\mathrm{OPT}$ is the error of the best-fitting halfspace for $f$. Previously, even with membership queries, the best known running time was $n^{\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)}$, achieved by the sample-based algorithm of Kalai, Klivans, Mansour, and Servedio (FOCS 2005). Our algorithm is the first agnostic halfspace learner under the uniform distribution on $\{\pm1\}^n$ whose running time is polynomial in $n$ with an exponent independent of $\varepsilon$. Combining our algorithm with a boosting argument yields a proper agnostic learner using only random examples. It achieves the same $\mathrm{OPT}+\varepsilon$ guarantee, with running time matching that of Kalai et al.\ up to an additive term depending only on $\varepsilon$. To our knowledge, this is the first sample-based proper agnostic learner in the Boolean setting with running time $2^{o(n)}$ for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$.
item.dc:creator: Anindya De, Elchanan Mossel, Shivam Nadimpalli, Joe Neeman

item.title: State Synthesis with an NP oracle
item.description: arXiv:2611.02370v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this note, I describe a quantum algorithm that prepares an arbitrary state $|\psi\rangle$ to inverse exponential precision in polynomial time by making queries to an $\mathsf{NP}$ oracle, assuming one can directly query entries of the state vector corresponding to $|\psi\rangle$. The previous best upper bound on the complexity class required by an oracle for this task was $\mathsf{PP}$. I provide evidence that $\mathsf{NP}$ is the best possible upper bound by showing that any quantum algorithm using a $\mathsf{P}$ oracle, or even a $\mathsf{P/poly}$ oracle, requires exponentially many queries. I also discuss some implications of this result for the $\mathsf{QMA}$ search-to-decision problem and unitary synthesis.
item.dc:creator: Aniruddha Sen

item.title: Circuit Lower Bounds for Extended Gate Bases from Subexponential Counting
item.description: arXiv:2611.02560v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study circuit lower bounds for extended gate bases using exact CNF counting and an extension-ring form of the contraction theorem of OpenAI. The deterministic counting theorem of Claude (Anthropic) yields an $\mathsf{E}^{\mathsf{NP}}$ language requiring $\Omega(m\sqrt{\log m}/\log\log m)$ gates over unbounded AND/OR with binary XOR, infinitely often. Using that contraction theorem, a bounded binary base with a linear budget of arbitrary XOR and symmetric gates requires $\Omega(m\sqrt{\log m})$ gates infinitely often. These results extend the binary-gate lower bound of OpenAI. Signed long-clause selectors reduce the first counting problem to the difference of two ordinary 3-CNF counts. Affine characters and unit-separated interpolation give the second counting interface, with logarithmic cost per symmetric-gate arity. A quantitative local-reduction transfer accounts for auxiliary variables, branch counts, and integer recovery.
item.dc:creator: Mengyang Wu, Minghao Wang

item.title: Information Complexity of Inner Product and Matrix Multiplication via Shannon-to-Min-Entropy Conversion
item.description: arXiv:2611.02684v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We determine the information complexity of matrix multiplication over finite fields under independent uniform inputs, up to a universal additive constant. The binary inner-product case resolves the open question of Braverman, Garg, Pankratov, and Weinstein on the optimal dependence of information complexity on the error probability. For inputs in $\mathbb F_2^m$ and error at most $\varepsilon\in[0,1/2]$, the information complexity with output at Bob lies between $(1-2\varepsilon)m-c_0$ and $(1-2\varepsilon)m$, where $c_0<4.772$ is a universal constant. For independent uniform matrices $X\in\mathbb F_q^{t\times m}$ and $Y\in\mathbb F_q^{s\times m}$, where $t\le s$, computing $XY^{\mathsf T}$ with output at Bob and error at most $\varepsilon\in[0,1]$ has information complexity $(1-q^{ts}\varepsilon/(q^{ts}-1))^+mt\log_2q$, up to an additive gap of less than $9.544$ bits. This gap is independent of the matrix dimensions, field size, and error. At zero error, the information complexity is exactly $mt\log_2q$. The information lower bounds for both inner product and matrix multiplication follow from a new Shannon-to-min-entropy theorem for convolution on discrete groups. Let $Q_1,\ldots,Q_k$ be the finitely supported distributions of independent random variables taking values in a discrete group, and let $s$ be the largest support size. We show that if $k\ge\lceil\lfloor\log_2s\rfloor\ln2\rceil$, then the min-entropy of their ordered product is at least the average Shannon entropy of the $Q_i$ minus $c_0$ bits. This holds for arbitrary discrete groups, including infinite and noncommutative groups, even when the input distributions differ. The leading coefficient of the logarithmic threshold is optimal.
item.dc:creator: Xiaohong Cai, Mingyang Zhu

item.title: Iterated Narrow Networks: Turing Completeness at Width 4 on Convex Input Spaces and the Complexity of Verification
item.description: arXiv:2611.02840v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the iterates of a fixed ReLU network $N$ of width 4, that is, the discrete-time system $x_{k+1} = N(x_k)$ on $[0,1]^4$. Equivalently, $x_k$ is the output of a weight-tied network made of $k$ copies of $N$, or of a recurrent network with no external input, started at $x_0$. We prove that every deterministic Turing machine $M$ admits such a network $N_M$. The network can be constructed in polynomial time from $M$. Each iteration has depth $\mathrm{poly}(|M|)$. The iterates of $N_M$ simulate $M$ exactly on every encoded tape. The number of iterations is proportional to the running time of $M$. Moreover, the fourth coordinate irreversibly flags every point of the convex cube $[0,1]^4$ whose simulation reads an invalid digit. This flag is the certificate that makes hardness reductions sound on convex input regions, the regime of practical verifiers. Convex regions were previously inaccessible because of a continuity obstruction inherent to ReLU networks. The correspondence has three consequences. First, reachability for iterated width-4 ReLU networks spans the full complexity hierarchy along the single axis of the time bound: it is NP-complete for a unary bound, NEXP-complete for a binary bound and RE-complete (undecidable) with no bound. Second, two extra neurons of width suffice to extend the hardness to every common smooth activation: at width 6, the robust verification problem (a promise problem with $\delta/2\delta$ gap) is NP-complete for $\tanh$, sigmoid, GELU, Swish, ELU, and any polynomial-time-computable continuous non-polynomial activation with a polynomial-time-computable Lipschitz constant. Third, the whole spectrum transfers to discretized Neural ODEs in dimension 5.
item.dc:creator: Olivier Bournez, Johanne Cohen, Adrian Wurm

item.title: Full-Rank Constructions of Explicit Lossless Expanders and Good Small-Set qLTCs
item.description: arXiv:2611.02963v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We construct explicit two-sided lossless expanders whose binary adjacency matrices have full rank, and use them to obtain explicit asymptotically good quantum LDPC codes whose specified X- and Z-check matrices have full row rank and satisfy small-set soundness, or confinement, on a linear range. Our lossless expanders are a variant of those of Hsieh, Lubotzky, Mohanty, Reiner, and Zhang, with a free action of a finite 2-group. Under such an action, injectivity and surjectivity of the adjacency matrix are detected on a fixed-size matrix indexed by vertex orbits. Adding a sparse factor to the gadget at the middle vertices of a single type then enforces full rank, with a controlled loss in expansion. To obtain the 2-group action, we observe that reducing the generators of the Lubotzky-Phillips-Sarnak Ramanujan graphs modulo powers of 2, instead of modulo an odd prime, gives Ramanujan Cayley graphs on finite 2-groups. This construction may be of independent interest. Plugging two such expanders into the balanced product of Lin and Hsieh gives the quantum codes, since full rank of the input graphs is inherited by the check matrices. Our construction supplies the code family sought by Hong, Guo, and Lucas. Applying their analysis, within their framework and under their dynamical assumptions, gives quantum memories whose free-energy density is analytic at every positive temperature and whose guaranteed lifetime is $exp(\Omega(N))$ at sufficiently low fixed positive temperature, where N is the blocklength. This improves the previously guaranteed stretched-exponential timescale.
item.dc:creator: Yali Aharon-Holzman, Michael Ilan, Assaf Reiner, Amnon Ta-Shma

item.title: Worst-Case to Average-Case Reductions for Basic Linear Algebra
item.description: arXiv:2611.03058v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study worst-case to average-case reductions for basic linear-algebraic problems over finite fields. A seminal work of Blum, Luby, and Rubinfeld established that any algorithm that successfully multiplies more than $75\%$ of matrix pairs over any finite field, implies an algorithm with essentially the same running time multiplying any pair of matrices. A sequence of follow-ups reduced the needed fraction of successful input pairs to any positive constant. Despite most of the other basic linear algebraic operations being computationally equivalent to matrix multiplication in the worst case, no such worst-case to average-case reductions were known for them. Recently, Vaikuntanathan and Zamir introduced a cryptographic primitive called trapdoor matrices and used them to prove such worst-case to average-case reductions for matrix inversion, solving a linear system, and computing the determinant, all conditioned on common cryptographic assumptions. Our main result is the first unconditional time-preserving worst-case to average-case reduction for matrix inversion. Any algorithm that correctly inverts any constant positive fraction of uniformly random invertible matrices implies a worst-case such algorithm. We also significantly strengthen the conditional reductions based on trapdoored matrices: We establish reductions for deciding invertibility and computing rank at the optimal success thresholds, and qualitatively improve the success threshold needed in the reduction for determinant computation---while previous reductions all required the success probability to be at least $1/2$, we show that any fixed positive average-case success probability suffices for exact worst-case determinant computation over infinitely many finite fields.
item.dc:creator: Or Zamir

item.title: Reed-Muller Codes are Optimal Binary Linear 3-Query LCCs
item.description: arXiv:2611.03145v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We prove that any linear $3$-query locally correctable code $C \colon \mathbb{F}_2^k \to \mathbb{F}_2^n$ with constant correction radius must have length $n \geq 2^{\Omega(\sqrt{k})}$. This improves on the prior best lower bound of $2^{\Omega(\sqrt{k/\log k})}$, due to [AG24], and shows that the folklore construction of linear $3$-LCCs from Reed-Muller codes, which achieve length $n = 2^{O(\sqrt{k})}$, is optimal up to constant factors in the exponent. Our proof builds on the approach of [KM24a], further refined in [Yan24,KM24b], that uses "chain derived equations" in combination with Kikuchi graphs. The crux of our argument is to show that a certain edge-coloured Kikuchi graph has a unique colour cycle: a cycle in which some colour is used exactly once. We do this by controlling the distribution of colours at each vertex in the graph using a random walk mixing argument and a novel hypergraph decomposition based on edge expansion of the hypergraph's "flattening" into a graph.
item.dc:creator: Oliver Janzer, Peter Manohar

item.title: Dissecting Geometric Constraints in Grokking: Interaction-Dependent Acceleration in Modular Arithmetic
item.description: arXiv:2611.03156v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Spherical transformer configurations can accelerate grokking through simultaneous modifications of several model properties. The present study investigated the contributions of these modifications in the published Sphere+Fourier configuration using 960 controlled modular-arithmetic runs. A complete factorial analysis varied residual projection, readout weight normalization, logit scale, and weight decay. Across four matched settings with weight decay, the successful-run mean crossing times without projection were 8-37 times those observed with projection. However, residual projection was insufficient to induce grokking without additional interventions. Various other unprojected configurations also generalized. Since projection altered the magnitude entering the readout, these comparisons could not separate geometry from output scale. A separate 100-run fixed-horizon study demonstrated faster first crossing for the complete configuration across five train/test partitions. Faster crossing did not necessarily correspond to greater persistence over extended training. Control experiments demonstrated rapid grokking without Fourier initialization. Task and depth sweeps also identified conditions in which the configuration failed to reach the criterion by 50K epochs. Accordingly, the observed acceleration depended on interactions among the components and did not extend uniformly across the tested tasks or depths.
item.dc:creator: Zachary A. Hampton, Wasiq Khan, Bilal Khan

item.title: Subpolynomial-Query Proximal Sampling Beyond Log-Concavity
item.description:
arXiv:2611.03442v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the gradient query complexity of sampling from a density $\pi(x)\propto\mathrm{e}^{-V(x)}$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$, where $V$ has a $ eta$-Lipschitz gradient but need not be convex. Our approach uses the proximal sampler, which alternates Gaussian perturbation with sampling a position conditional on the noisy observation. We implement its observation chain using the high-order noisy conditional sampler of [OpenAI 2026], obtaining improved dimension dependence under functional inequalities. If $\pi$ satisfies a log-Sobolev inequality (LSI) with constant $\alpha$, then for every fixed $
u>0$, there is a finite constant $C_
u$ depending only on $
u$ such that the algorithm returns a sample within total-variation distance $\varepsilon$ using at most $C_
u\kappa(d+\kappa+\varepsilon^{-1}+\|
abla V(x_0)\|^2/ eta)^
u$ queries, where $\kappa= eta/\alpha$ and $x_0$ is an arbitrary reference point for initialization. The analysis controls center-dependent local errors along exact proximal histories and removes the final observation noise by conditional decoding. Under a Poincar'e inequality (PI), we obtain a corresponding guarantee from a warm start with a known bound on its R'enyi divergence. An oracle lower bound shows that a stationary point alone, which suffices under LSI, is insufficient under PI.
item.dc:creator: Wei Guo, Bo Yuan, Ye He, Jiaming Liang, Molei Tao, Yongxin Chen

item.title: Tilted Convexity and an Exact Offline-Online Separation
item.description: arXiv:2611.03472v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Convexity has three equivalent descriptions: support by affine functions, monotonicity of the subdifferential, and increasing secant slopes. We weaken all three by one distortion with parameter $\gamma\in(0,1]$, which multiplies positive changes by $\gamma$ and divides negative ones by $\gamma$. The resulting classes are the convex functions at $\gamma=1$ and, for $\gamma<1$, are distinct and nested, with the parameter dropping by at most a square along the chain. For proper lower semicontinuous functions in these classes, the effective domain is convex, local minimizers are global, and the function is locally Lipschitz on the relative interior of its domain. The classes separate offline from online optimization over compact convex sets with efficient projection, with access to function values and bounded support vectors. A smooth member of any class can be minimized to additive accuracy $\varepsilon$ with $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$ first-order queries and projections. Online, with nonpositive losses and $\alpha$-regret measured against $\alpha$ times the best fixed point, a polynomial-time algorithm achieves $\gamma$-regret $O(\sqrt T)$ on the largest class. For every fixed, effectively specified $\gamma\in(0,1)$ and every $\alpha\in(\gamma,1]$, no randomized polynomial-time algorithm has sublinear expected $\alpha$-regret unless $\mathbf{NP}=\mathbf{RP}$, already for smooth concave polynomial losses in the smallest class, each minimized by one linear optimization. Thus, unless $\mathbf{NP}=\mathbf{RP}$, $\gamma$ is the exact online coefficient of each class, while the offline coefficient is one.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Pedramfar, Rajiv Khanna, Christopher John Quinn, Vaneet Aggarwal

item.title: Get Permanent Results Faster by Counting Stars
item.description: arXiv:2611.03636v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We show that $n \times n$ permanents can be computed with $O^*{(2-\varepsilon)^n}$ arithmetic operations over every commutative ring, for $\varepsilon = 10^{-40}$. This solves a problem stated in Knuth's The Art of Computer Programming. Our algorithm implements the classical Binet--Minc identity with dynamic programming and careful bookkeeping. It also gives algebraic branching programs of size $O^*{(2-\varepsilon)^n}$.
item.dc:creator: Radu Curticapean

item.title: Enumerating Complexity Revisited
item.description: arXiv:2312.04187v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the relation between deterministic and randomized $\textit{enumerating}$ Kolmogorov complexity of sets $S\subseteq \mathbb{N}$. Let $D(S)$ be the length of a shortest input on which a fixed optimal deterministic machine enumerates $S$, and let $ R(S) $ be the probability that a fixed optimal randomized machine enumerates $S$. It is easy to see that $-\log R(S) \le D(S)+O(\log D(S))$ for every $S$; the converse direction is much harder. Solovay proved $D(S)\le -3\log R(S) +O(\log\log\frac{1}{ R(S) })$ for all $S$, while for finite sets the sharper bound with the constant $2$ is known. We show that the case of infinite sets carries no extra cost: $\textit{any}$ inequality of the form $D(F)\le -\alpha\log R(F)+O(\log\log\frac{1}{R(F)})$ with a computable $\alpha$, valid for all finite $F$, automatically extends to all sets. More generally, we prove a single dichotomy from which such transfer results follow for an arbitrary computable non-decreasing bound, and which also shows that every c.e. set $S$ has a finite subset $F$ such that $F$ has at least as large deterministic complexity as $S$ but randomized one approximately the same or lower. Our result makes qualitative progress on a problem studied by Solovay in 1977 by showing that the search for the optimal constant can be reduced to a purely combinatorial question about a game played with finite sets. In particular, our result yields $D(S)\le-2\log R(S) +O(\log\log\frac{1}{ R(S) })$ for every $S$, improving Solovay's constant $3$ to $2$.
item.dc:creator: Alexander Shekhovtsov, Georgii Zakharov, Nikolay Vereshchagin

item.title: More on Higher Order Busy Beaver Functions
item.description: arXiv:2507.20321v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we extend the Busy Beaver function to a class of higher order Busy Beaver functions based on Turing oracle machine. We prove some results about the relation between decidability of number theoretical formula and higher order Busy Beaver functions, and the relations between computability of max-min partial recursive functions, limit partial recursive functions and higher order Busy Beaver functions. We also present some conjectures on higher order Busy Beaver functions.
item.dc:creator: Zining Cao

item.title: Optimal PRGs for Low-Degree Polynomials over Polynomial-Size Fields
item.description: arXiv:2602.10030v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We construct the first pseudorandom generator (PRG) with optimal seed length for degree-$d$ polynomials over fields of size $q \approx d^4$, with no restriction on the characteristic. This improves on the construction of Dwivedi, Guo, and Volk (RANDOM 2024), which requires fields of size exponential in $d$ and sufficiently large characteristic, and on that of Derksen and Viola (FOCS 2022), which requires a field size that grows with the number of variables $n$. A recent breakthrough by Chattopadhyay, Hatami, Lee, Lovett, Tal, and Viola (ECCC 2026) gives a PRG over the binary field with seed length $\widetilde{O}(d^2\log^2 n)$, with subsequent work by Cohen (ECCC 2026) achieving seed length $O(d^4\log n)$. Both constructions use polarized random walks, and the current analyses incur at least a quadratic dependence on $d$. Our second result is a reduction that provides an alternative route to nearly optimal seed length over the binary field through improved constructions over larger fields. Specifically, we prove that, for any $\delta \in (0,1)$, an optimal-seed PRG for degree-$d$ polynomials over fields of characteristic two and size $q \approx d^\delta$ would yield a PRG over the binary field with seed length $O(d^{1/(1-\delta)}\log n)$.
item.dc:creator: Gil Cohen, Noam Goldgraber

item.title: The program is still there, and searching for it obeys a conservation law
item.description: arXiv:2606.13799v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The length of the shortest program that generates a sequence, its Kolmogorov complexity, is uncomputable, so we ask what finding a short program costs when one exists. Many search algorithms, including Levin search, evolutionary methods, simulated annealing and the cross-entropy method, learn about a candidate program only through its score, how much of the sequence it reproduces. For such algorithms we define the coupling width of a search problem, the largest number of program fields that must change together before the score moves. We prove an unconditional worst-case lower bound on the number of candidates scored, exponential in that width. Under stated conditions, a conservation law follows, in which each bit of structural knowledge injected into a search removes at most one bit of search. The structure plus the logarithm of the remaining search is at least a fixed fraction of the sequence's Kolmogorov complexity. That fraction tends to one as the instruction set grows, so the lower bound approaches Levin's 1973 upper bound, apart from the program's running time. Search by score must pay this cost to be complete. We prove that our engine's structural inference avoids it only by giving up coverage, as does, if one-way functions exist, every method that runs in polynomial time. Our deterministic engine, built on this theory, recovers a generating program, certified by compressing its data and predicting an unseen continuation, for 2,383 of 3,914 candidate sequences in four populations of integer sequences and cellular automata, including the chaotic Rule 30.
item.dc:creator: Jorge Miguel Silva

item.title: A Forward-Backward Weight Analysis of INW for Permutation Branching Programs
item.description: arXiv:2607.18168v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We construct an $\varepsilon$-error PRG for permutation read-once branching programs of length $n$ and width $w$ with seed length \[ O\left((\log w+\log(1/\varepsilon))\cdot \log n\right). \] This gives an exponential improvement in the dependence on $w$ compared with the constructions of De (CCC 2011) and Steinke (ECCC 2012). Compared with the work of Braverman, Rao, Raz, and Yehudayoff (FOCS 2010; SICOMP 2014), which applies more generally to regular branching programs and already achieves the optimal dependence on $w$, our result improves the dependence on the length $n$, attaining the optimal logarithmic dependence. The generator itself is the classical INW PRG of Impagliazzo, Nisan, and Wigderson (STOC 1994). We show that, for permutation branching programs, the INW generator can be instantiated with expanders whose degrees are polynomial in $w$ and $1/\varepsilon$ and, crucially, independent of $n$. To prove this, we analyze error propagation using program-dependent seminorms tailored to the branching program at hand. These seminorms build on the weight function introduced by Braverman et al. The key point is that, when measured in these adapted seminorms, the error does not accumulate throughout the recursion. Since our analysis relies only on the spectral expansion of the underlying expanders, our seed length tightly matches the recent lower bound for spectral analyses of the INW generator due to Hoza, Pyne, and Vadhan (Algorithmica 2024).
item.dc:creator: Gil Cohen, Dean Doron, Noam Goldgraber

item.title: Algebraic-Geometric Parvaresh--Vardy Subspace Designs and Rank Condensers
item.description: arXiv:2609.32834v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A subspace design is a collection of subspaces $H_1,\ldots,H_n$ of $\mathbb{F}_q^k$ with the property that no low-dimensional subspace $W$ intersects the collection "too much". Subspace designs and related objects in linear-algebraic pseudorandomness have found a broad range of applications, ranging from list decoding to derandomizing algorithms. We construct explicit strong subspace designs over every finite field. In the extremal case where the co-dimension $t$ of each $H_i$ is equal to the dimension of $W$, for every constant field size our construction attains $n=\Omega(k)$ and matches the probabilistic intersection bound up to a constant factor. All previous constructions required the field size to grow with $t$ (or $k$). Our subspace designs also imply new constructions of rank condensers over arbitrary finite fields. This result is the first to achieve an optimal dependence on $k$ while maintaining both a constant output entropy rate and a constant field size. As an application, we construct lossless rank extractors for linear sources of rank $r$, for all $r < q$, with parameters matching those of Guo, Raj, Shangguan and Zhang (FOCS '26), thereby generalizing their result to prime fields and smaller field sizes. Our construction is based on an algebraic-geometric version of the Parvaresh--Vardy codes (Parvaresh--Vardy FOCS '05, Guruswami ECCC '05), extending the framework underlying the condensers of Guruswami, Umans and Vadhan (JACM '09). We view our construction as a linear-algebraic analysis -- tailored to affine sources -- of the GUV construction, generalized to functions over algebraic curves. More specifically, inspired by Ta-Shma and Umans (CCC '12) we develop a two-level evaluation scheme, where we first evaluate a function on a curve at extension-field points, and then evaluate a corresponding affine-linear polynomial to obtain outputs over the base field.
item.dc:creator: Gil Cohen, Dean Doron, Noam Goldgraber

item.title: NP-hardness of additive approximation for generalized Tur\'{a}n problems
item.description: arXiv:2610.16358v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Given a graph $T$ and a nonempty family $\mathcal{F}$ of graphs, let $\operatorname{ex}(G, T, \mathcal{F})$ denote the maximum number of copies of $T$ in an $\mathcal{F}$-free subgraph of a host graph $G$. Alon and Shikhelman [Algorithmica, 2022] conjectured that if $e(T)> 0$ and no member of $\mathcal{F}$ is a subgraph of a blow-up of $T$, then for every $\varepsilon>0$, approximating $\operatorname{ex}(G, T, \mathcal{F})$ within an additive error of $n^{v(T)-\varepsilon}$ is NP-hard for an input graph $G$ on $n$ vertices. Previous advances toward this conjecture include the resolution of the canonical case $T=K_2$ by Alon, Shapira, and Sudakov [Ann. of Math., 2009], as well as the case of $\operatorname{ex}(G,K_m,K_k)$ by Alon and Shikhelman. In this paper, we confirm this conjecture for every bipartite graph $T$ and every clique $T$. Our proof reductions combine several techniques, including iterative leaf additions, symmetric rooted extensions, and random transversals. Together, they encode the optimal value of the NP-hard Max $r$-Colorable Subgraph problem into the objectives $\operatorname{ex}(G, T, \mathcal{F})$ for a suitably constructed graph $G$.
item.dc:creator: Yihan Chen, Jialin He, Xihe Li, Jie Ma, Tianying Xie

item.title: Unconditional Lower Bounds for the Fredman--Khachiyan Algorithms for Monotone Boolean Duality Testing
item.description: arXiv:2610.34474v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We prove unconditional lower bounds on the number of recursive calls made by the two algorithms of Fredman and Khachiyan (1996) for monotone Boolean duality testing, as a function of the explicit input size $N$. For Algorithm A we show a lower bound of $N^{\Omega(\log N)}$ on the dual pairs $(\HH_k,\LL_k)$ obtained from the read-once family of Gurvich and Khachiyan. The proof lower-bounds the number of leaves of every binary decision tree computing the function by the modulus of its multilinear polynomial evaluated at a complex point of the unit circle. It therefore applies to every choice of branching variables and, more generally, to the class of two-child variable-restriction procedures whose terminal calls have polynomially bounded decision-tree complexity. On this family the number of calls is exactly $N^{\Theta(\log N)}$. For Algorithm B, a symmetric specialization of the polynomial padding construction of Kobayashi, Kurita, and Wasa, with full polynomial blocks, yields at least $q^{(t-1)k-t(t-1)/2}$ calls, where $k=4t^2$ and $q=\Theta(t^2)$; as a function of $N$ this is $N^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log N/\log\log N})}$ along an infinite family. In an appendix we show that applying the padding construction directly to Algorithm A gives $\Omega(2^n)$ calls on a dual pair obtained from an unsatisfiable $n$-variable formula, which is only $N^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log N/\log\log N})}$ in terms of the input size. No complexity-theoretic assumption is used. The proofs allow every branching-variable choice permitted by the respective algorithm. They concern the original recursive procedures, counting every invocation separately, without sharing calls or adding positive stopping tests.
item.dc:creator: Khaled Elbassioni

item.title: A Witnessing Duality for ReLU Network Depth
item.description: arXiv:2610.38281v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A depth lower bound for ReLU networks asserts that every sufficiently shallow network fails on some input. What does a proof of such a bound compute? We study this question for exact computation of the maximum of $n$ real inputs, with depth measured by the number of hidden layers. For every separately fixed prime $q$ and depth bound $K$, we give a uniform $\mathsf{TC}^0$ refuter for rational networks with at most $K$ hidden layers and more than $q^K$ inputs, provided that the reduced denominators of their nonbias weights are not divisible by $q$. Biases may be arbitrary rationals. The refuter finds a rational input on which the network fails, and its correctness is provable in $\mathbf{VTC}^0$, the bounded-arithmetic theory of uniform constant-depth threshold computation. The underlying numerical depth lower bound follows from Averkov, Hojny and Merkert (ICLR 2025), extending Haase, Hertrich and Loho (ICLR 2023); our contribution is an internal proof that makes its geometric argument into a feasible refuter. On the construction side, $\mathbf{VTC}^0$ verifies locally checkable certificates for the balanced integer-weight maximum network of depth $\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$. At $q=2$, the construction and refuter meet: for each fixed $K$, the theory verifies that integer-nonbias-weight networks with arbitrary rational biases can compute the maximum with at most $K$ hidden layers exactly when $n\le 2^K$. We also give certified rational constructions of polynomial encoding length and depth $O(\log n/\log\log n)$. These results instantiate a witnessing duality: bounded proofs of certified existence and of refutation correspond, respectively, to threshold-computable constructors and refuters whose guarantees the theory proves.
item.dc:creator: Dimitrios Myrisiotis

item.title: One Polynomial Field for Every Euler Step and the Flow: Polynomial Dynamics for P and PSPACE
item.description: arXiv:2610.40025v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We construct, for each deterministic Turing machine that halts on all inputs, one polynomial vector field with rational coefficients that performs the same logical computation at unit Euler step, at every smaller or variable step in $(0,1]$ with divergent sum, and along the flow. This unifies discrete-time and continuous-time computation by polynomial dynamics, which earlier characterizations treated separately. For a machine making $T$ transitions in space $H$, a logical scale $h=2^{-s}$ with $s=O(H)$ suffices, with physical time $O(s(T+s))$, drift disturbances up to $h^{2K}$ for a fixed exponent $K$, and $2Ks+3$ fractional bits at unit step.
