On a fixed compact domain, polynomial time and robust eventual decision characterize P and PSPACE, respectively, with polynomial scale thresholds and no supplied stabilization horizon in the space case. Without sign, floor or conditional primitives, margin amplification at bounded speed, overlapping polynomial gates and interval-product estimates give the common realization, from which we derive shared logical traces, fixed-field PSPACE-complete prediction and a robust safety family with polynomial certificates common to all Euler steps and the flow.
item.dc:creator: Olivier Bournez

item.title: Counting Square Tilings with a Fixed Set of Polyominoes Is #EXP-Complete
item.description: arXiv:2610.42063v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: An important question in counting complexity is whether exact counting can remain hard under restrictions that make feasibility easy. Tilings of squares by a fixed family of polyominoes provide a stringent test of this question, since tileability is polynomial-time decidable and the only varying input is a binary-encoded side length. We prove that there exists a fixed finite family of connected polyominoes for which counting translation-only square tilings is #EXP-complete under polynomial-time metric reductions, while the counting function belongs to #E. The resulting separation reveals that solution multiplicities can retain computational information that feasibility alone cannot capture. The proof develops a two-stage numerical isolation technique that combines a boundary-amplified Wang system with a rigid geometric compiler to recover accepting-computation counts while controlling all noncanonical tilings.
item.dc:creator: Qiuyu Chen, Baao Xie

item.title: Approximate Polynomial Satisfiability and Integral Closure Membership in the Counting Hierarchy
item.description: arXiv:2610.42138v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Andrews, Garg, and Schost (FOCS~2026) recently, in a breakthrough result, placed Hilbert's Nullstellensatz (HN) in the Counting Hierarchy ($\CH$) using constant-depth circuits for multivariate resultants. While HN deals with exact polynomial satisfiability, Guo, Saxena, and Sinhababu (CCC~2018; Theory of Computing~2019) introduced approximate polynomial satisfiability (APS) as a natural approximative analogue of polynomial system satisfiability. They proved its $\mathsf{NP}$-hardness and a $\PSPACE$ upper bound, and used APS to construct hitting sets for $\overline{\mathsf{VP}}$ in polynomial space, substantially narrowing the GCT chasm in geometric complexity theory. We place APS in the Counting Hierarchy for rational polynomials given by arithmetic circuits. Our proof combines Noether normalization with a geometric restriction on how points in the image of a polynomial map approach the origin, reducing APS to a test on multivariate resultants which allows solvability in $\CH$. It complements the independent and concurrent proofs of Balaji, Shirmohammadi, Tavenas, and Worrell, and Andrews, Garg, Oliveira, and Schost. Moreover, we also place integral closure membership testing in the Counting Hierarchy. Here, the question is whether a given polynomial $f$ is integral over $\C[f_1,\ldots,f_m]$. Our approach uses a global annihilator criterion and an effective degree bound to reduce non-integrality to APS in polynomial time. In fact, we show that the reduction holds both ways, and Integral Closure Membership Testing is equivalent to APS under polynomial-time reductions.
item.dc:creator: Sanyam Agarwal, Archit Hari, Anurag Pandey, Himanshu Shukla

item.title: Tight (Double) Exponential Bounds for Identification Problems: Locating-Dominating Set and Test Cover
item.description: arXiv:2402.08346v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We investigate fine-grained algorithmic aspects for classical identification problems in graphs, namely LOCATING-DOMINATING SET, and in set systems, namely TEST COVER. In the first problem, an input is a graph $G$ on $n$ vertices and an integer $k$, and the objective is to decide whether there is a subset $S$ of $k$ vertices such that any two distinct vertices not in $S$ are dominated by distinct subsets of $S$. In the second problem, an input is a set $U$ of items, a collection $\mathcal{F}$ of subsets of $U$ called tests, and an integer $k$, and the objective is to select a set $S$ of at most $k$ tests such that any two distinct items are contained in a distinct subset of tests of $S$. For our first result, we show that LOCATING-DOMINATING SET (respectively, TEST COVER) parameterized by the treewidth of the input graph (respectively, the incidence graph) does not admit an algorithm running in time $2^{2^{o(\textsf{tw})}} \cdot {\rm poly}(n)$ (respectively, $2^{2^{o(\textsf{tw})}} \cdot {\rm poly}(|U| + |\mathcal{F}|)$), unless the ETH fails. Next, we prove that, unless the ETH fails, LOCATING-DOMINATING SET does not admit an algorithm running in time $2^{o(k^2)} \cdot {\rm poly}(n)$, nor a polynomial-time kernelization algorithm that reduces the solution size and outputs a kernel with $2^{o(k)}$ vertices, and TEST COVER does not admit an algorithm running in time $2^{2^{o(k)}} \cdot {\rm poly}(|U| + |\mathcal{F}|)$ nor a kernel with $2^{2^{o(k)}}$ vertices. Again, we show that these lower bounds are tight by designing (kernelization) algorithms with matching running times.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: SIAM Journal on Discrete Mathematics, Vol. 40(3), 2026
item.dc:creator: Dipayan Chakraborty, Florent Foucaud, Diptapriyo Majumdar, Prafullkumar Tale

item.title: Structures preserved by primitive actions of $S_\omega$
item.description: arXiv:2501.03789v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present a dichotomy for structures $A$ that are preserved by primitive actions of $S_{\omega} = \text{Sym}({\mathbb N})$: such a structure primitively positively constructs all finite structures and the constraint satisfaction problem is NP-complete, or the constraint satisfaction problem for $A$ is in P. To prove our result, we study the first-order reducts of the Johnson graph $J(k)$, for $k \geq 2$, whose automorphism group $G$ equals the action of $\text{Sym}({\mathbb N})$ on the set $V$ of $k$-element subsets of $\mathbb N$. We use the fact that $J(k)$ has a finitely bounded homogeneous Ramsey expansion and that $G$ is a maximal closed subgroup of $\text{Sym}(V)$.
item.dc:creator: Manuel Bodirsky, Bertalan Bodor

item.title: A SPIDER-type stochastic subgradient method for expectation-constrained nonconvex nonsmooth optimization
item.description: arXiv:2501.19214v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Many real-world problems, such as those with fairness constraints, involve complex expectation constraints and large datasets, necessitating the design of efficient stochastic methods to solve them. Most existing research focuses on cases with no {constraint} or easy-to-project constraints or deterministic constraints. In this paper, we consider nonconvex nonsmooth stochastic optimization problems with expectation constraints, for which we build a novel exact penalty model. We first show the relationship between the penalty model and the original problem. Then on solving the penalty problem, we present a single-loop SPIDER-type stochastic subgradient method, which utilizes the subgradients of both the objective and constraint functions, as well as the constraint function value at each iteration. Under certain regularity conditions (weaker than Slater-type constraint qualification or strong feasibility assumed in existing works), we establish an iteration complexity result of $O(\epsilon^{-4})$ to reach a near-$\epsilon$ stationary point of the penalized problem in expectation, matching the lower bound for such tasks. Building on the exact penalization, an $(\epsilon,\epsilon)$-KKT point of the original problem is obtained. For a few scenarios, our complexity of either the {objective} sample subgradient or the constraint sample function values can be lower than the state-of-the-art results by a factor of $\epsilon^{-2}$. Moreover, on solving two fairness-constrained problems and a multi-class Neyman-Pearson classification problem, our method is significantly (up to 466 times) faster than the state-of-the-art algorithms, including switching subgradient method and inexact proximal point methods.
item.dc:creator: Wei Liu, Yangyang Xu

item.title: Matrices with displacement structure: a deterministic approach for linear systems and nullspace bases
item.description: arXiv:2603.02425v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: For matrices with a displacement structure, the fastest known algorithms for solving linear systems and computing nullspace bases are randomized, with respective costs of $\tilde{O}(\alpha^{\omega-1} n)$ and $\tilde{O}(\alpha^2 n)$ operations in the base field. Here $n \times n$ is the matrix size, $\alpha$ is its displacement rank, $\omega > 2$ is a feasible exponent for matrix multiplication, and $\tilde{O}(\cdot)$ hides logarithmic factors. For a long time, such structured solvers were also the fastest known method to perform Hermite-Pad\'e or simultaneous Pad\'e approximations, and their interpolation variants, until recently when these problems received efficient and deterministic solutions via polynomial matrix algorithms. This work proposes to take the converse direction, by showing that these recent polynomial matrix tools can be used to improve structured matrix computations. We present a new approach which, for the Toeplitz-like, Vandermonde-like, and Cauchy-like structures, solves linear systems and computes nullspace bases in $\tilde{O}(\alpha^{\omega-1}(m+n))$ operations for an arbitrary $m \times n$ matrix, deterministically and with no assumption on the base field. This bound matches the best known randomized one for linear systems and improves upon it for nullspaces. The approach reformulates the problem as a modular equation on univariate polynomials, and describes all its solutions in three steps: computing a basis of solutions to a vector M-Pad\'e approximation problem, solving a polynomial matrix equation to get rid of unwanted unknowns, and finding the sought unknowns via simultaneous M-Pad\'e approximation.
item.dc:creator: Sara Khichane, Vincent Neiger

item.title: Identification to Subclasses of Chordal Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2604.24325v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: An identification of two vertices \(u\) and \(v\) in a graph replaces them with a new vertex that is made adjacent to every vertex of \(N(u)\cup N(v)\setminus \{u,v\}\). We study the \(\mathcal{H}\)-Identification problem, which is to decide whether a given graph \(G\) can be transformed (``identified'') to a graph in \(\mathcal{H}\) by applying at most \(k\) vertex identifications. We determine the classical and parameterized complexity of this problem for various subclasses \(\mathcal{H}\) of chordal graphs, obtaining an almost complete picture for two parameters: \(k\) and \(n-k\). We also consider the Identification problem, which is to test, for two given graphs \(G\) and \(H\), whether \(G\) can be identified to \(H\). We determine the parameterized complexity of this problem when \(H\) is a graph from one of our testbed classes, taking the number of simplicial vertices of \(H\) as the parameter.
item.dc:creator: Petr A. Golovach, Laure Morelle, Dani\"el Paulusma

item.title: Discrepancy for Random Linear Codes
item.description: arXiv:2606.24471v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We show that random linear codes (RLCs) possess nearly optimal discrepancy-type properties in a broad range of settings. Our main results are two general discrepancy theorems: one controls all translates of a fixed test, and the other controls large families of Fourier-pseudorandom tests. Two motivating examples follow: First, RLCs behave essentially like unstructured random codes for list-decoding from errors above capacity. More precisely, an RLC $C\subseteq \mathbb{F}_q^n$ of rate $1 - \frac{1}{n}\log_q|B_\rho| + \varepsilon$, where $|B_\rho|$ is the volume of a radius-$\rho$ Hamming ball in $\mathbb{F}_q^n$, satisfies $|C \cap B| = (1\pm o(1)) \frac{|C|\cdot |B|}{q^n}$ simultaneously for all radius-$\rho$ Hamming balls $B$ with high probability. This significantly strengthens the best prior results, which follow from work by Blinovsky (1987, 1990) and Levitin (1988) on the covering properties of RLCs. Second, over prime fields, RLCs behave essentially like unstructured random codes for zero-error list-recovery, and list-recovery from erasures, above capacity. More precisely, for a prime $q>2$ and input list size $2\leq \ell\leq q-1$, an RLC $C\subseteq \mathbb{F}_q^n$ of rate $1-\log_q \ell+\varepsilon$ will satisfy $|C \cap S| = (1\pm o(1)) \frac{|C|\cdot \ell^n}{q^n}$ simultaneously for all combinatorial rectangles $S=S_1\times S_2\times\cdots\times S_n$, where $|S_i|=\ell$ for all $i$, with high probability. An analogous result also holds when we can bound $|S_i|$ only for some of the $i$'s. We use this to show the abundance of locally leakage-resilient $n$-party linear ramp secret sharing schemes with any linear reconstruction threshold and sublinear threshold gap $O(n/\log n)$ over fields of polynomial size $q=\Theta(n^\gamma)$ for a constant $\gamma\in(0,1/5)$. Prior work was stuck at reconstruction thresholds above $n/2$ for both threshold and ramp schemes.
item.dc:creator: Dean Doron, Tal Leonov, Jonathan Mosheiff, Henrique Navas, Nicolas Resch, Jo\~ao Ribeiro

item.title: Exponential Quantum Advantage in Testing Fourier Dimensionality
item.description: arXiv:2609.25816v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A boolean function $f$ has Fourier dimension $k$ if its strings with nonzero Fourier coefficients span a subspace of dimension $k$. We first consider the property testing task of determining whether a function has Fourier dimension at most $k$, or is $\epsilon$-far from being so. We show that there is an $O(k/\sqrt{\epsilon})$-query quantum property tester for this problem, which we show to be almost optimal. Combined with Gopalan \etal's classical lower bound of $\Omega(2^{k/2})$, this demonstrates an exponential quantum advantage for this task. We complement this result with a $\tilde{O}(2^{k/2}/\epsilon)$ classical tester, giving a quadratic improvement over the previous best tester, and essentially settling the classical query complexity. We then introduce and study the tolerant version of this problem. That is, determining whether a function is $\alpha\epsilon$-close to having Fourier dimension at most $k$, or is $\epsilon$-far from being so. Perhaps surprisingly, we show that this tolerant version of the problem is essentially just as hard as the standard version of the problem. That is, we show this problem has a $\tilde{O}(k/\epsilon)$ quantum tester, and a $\tilde{O}(2^{k/2}/\epsilon)$ classical tester.
item.dc:creator: Kenny Chen

item.title: An Exponential Succinctness Gap between Three-Variable Logic and the Calculus of Relations
item.description: arXiv:2609.26778v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Three-variable first-order logic ($\mathrm{FO}^3$) and the calculus of relations (CoR) define the same binary queries, an equivalence that goes back to Tarski's work in the 1940s. The classical translation from $\mathrm{FO}^3$ to CoR is single-exponential, but it has remained open whether this blowup is necessary. We prove that it is, even over finite structures and even for circuits that share subterms. Our proof introduces a new technique: we modify a single finite structure in exponentially many local ways, each changing the answer of a short $\mathrm{FO}^3$ formula $\varphi$. In any CoR circuit $C$ equivalent to $\varphi$, only compositions of binary relations can notice these modifications, and each composition can notice at most two; thus, $C$ requires exponentially many compositions. The same technique gives an exponential succinctness gap between $\mathrm{FO}^3$ and $\mathrm{FO}^2$, and exponential lower bounds for matrix query languages over the Boolean and tropical semirings, where the analogous question was also open.
item.dc:creator: Yuya Uezato, Yoshiki Nakamura

item.title: Computational Bounds for $f$-Routing
item.description: arXiv:2609.40278v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The $f$-routing protocol is a leading candidate for quantum position verification (Kent, Munro, and Spiller, Physical Review A, 2011), but security guarantees for explicit functions remain limited. We prove unconditional resource lower bounds for uniform attackers. Our techniques bypass communication-complexity bounds central to previous works, which are inherently at most linear in the input length. We show that, for input length $n$ and a sufficiently small constant $\epsilon>0$, a uniform strategy running in time $T$ and succeeding with probability at least $1-\epsilon$ on every input implies the following computational bounds on $f$. 1. If the strategies are arbitrary quantum channels, then $f\in \mathrm{QSZK}(\mathrm{poly}(T))$, where $\mathrm{QSZK}(T)$ is the class of languages having quantum statistical zero-knowledge proofs in which the verifier runs in time $T$ and the simulator in time $\mathrm{poly}(T)$. 2. If the strategies are Clifford+T circuits using at most $t$ magic gates, then $f\in \mathrm{DTIME}(\mathrm{poly}(T2^t))$. 3. If the strategies are explicit Pauli-sparse unitaries acting on at most $T$ qubits and having at most $s$ nonzero Pauli coefficients, then $f\in \mathrm{DTIME}(\mathrm{poly}(Ts))$. Time and space hierarchies then yield explicit functions secure against superlinear and even all polynomial-time adversaries under our computational restrictions. These bounds exceed the bounded-storage qubit bound $q\leq\log n$ of Bluhm, Christandl, and Speelman (Nature Physics, 2022) for the inner product function $f=\mathrm{IP}$, at the cost of restricting adversarial computation and increasing honest evaluation complexity.
item.dc:creator: Oren Renard, Nicholas Spooner

item.title: Beyond light cones: State preparation complexity in quantum spin glasses
item.description: arXiv:2610.02166v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce a technique for studying state preparation complexity in the quantum $p$-spin model on $n$ qubits, a disordered quantum spin system with random interactions on every set of $p$ qubits. We reduce the task of proving state preparation lower bounds to bounding the local profile complexity of the class, a quantity derived from the metric entropy of the set of vectors recording each state's expectation values against all weight-$p$ Pauli strings. We show that, for sufficiently large fixed $p$, any class with local profile complexity $O(n^2)$ remains separated from the ground-state energy by $\Omega(\sqrt n)$, a gap on the leading energy scale. When the profile complexity is $o(n^2)$, we prove the stronger conclusion that the class cannot outperform a benchmark class of simpler states at leading order. Product states always provide such a benchmark. Our framework strengthens known bounds and covers classes beyond the reach of previous methods. These include examples where circuit lightcones extend across the entire system, preventing an application of standard arguments. We obtain an $\Omega(n^2/\log n)$ gate lower bound for preparing near-ground states and depth--width tradeoffs, allowing arbitrary one- and two-qubit gates and arbitrarily many discardable ancillas. We also derive lower bounds on entanglement depth and matrix product state bond dimension, and energy obstructions for forward and reverse magic at every fixed level of Parham's magic hierarchy (arXiv:2504.19966). For Clifford circuits doped with $T$-gates, we obtain sharper energy comparisons using product stabilizer states as a more restrictive benchmark. The proof combines an adaptation of a nonsymmetric quantum de Finetti theorem (arXiv:1810.12197) with metric-entropy bounds for the Gaussian process indexed by the local profiles of states in the class.

item.title: Lower Bounds for Parallel Diffusion Sampling
item.description: arXiv:2610.09166v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Standard diffusion samplers generate samples through sequential evaluations of a learned score function, with each query depending on previous answers. Parallel samplers seek to accelerate this process by making multiple score queries simultaneously. We ask how many adaptive rounds are necessary when each round allows polynomially many queries. We establish the first polynomial lower bounds on the round complexity of diffusion sampling with approximate scores satisfying a mean-square accuracy guarantee. Specifically, we prove (1) a $\widetilde{\Omega}(d^{1/3})$-round lower bound for sampling smooth, near-isotropic Gaussian mixtures in $\mathbb{R}^d$, and (2) a tight $\Omega(d)$-round lower bound for uniform sampling from anisotropic axis-aligned boxes contained in the unit ball. Both bounds hold for arbitrary randomized algorithms making polynomially many queries per round at arbitrary locations and noise levels, with inverse-polynomial score error and constant total variation accuracy. Our near-isotropic construction follows the blockwise approach of earlier lower bounds for parallel matroid search and discrete sampling \cite{KUW85,AGR24}. We use independent coordinate blocks containing random codebooks with well-separated rates and construct approximate score oracles whose responses in each block depend on consistency tests in earlier blocks. Together, the rate separation and these tests ensure that each round reveals information about at most one additional block with high probability.
item.dc:creator: Yiwen Kou, Yimeng Wang

item.title: Subset Sum via Partial Match
item.description: arXiv:2610.10446v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We show that the subset sum problem can be solved in randomized time $O(2^{0.49999\overline{7}n})$, breaking the $2^{n/2}$ meet-in-the-middle barrier. Our approach builds on the representation technique framework of Randolph and W\k{e}grzycki (STOC 2026). We choose a representation for which testing the compatibility of pairs of partial solution vectors is exactly the partial match problem. To beat exponent $1/2$ for subset sum, it then suffices to give a nontrivial partial match algorithm in a certain parameter regime. We achieve this by designing a depth-2 linear circuit for the partial match matrix, which yields an efficient algorithm via the framework of Alman and Li (FOCS 2025).
item.dc:creator: Baitian Li, Lixi Ye

item.title: Undirected Multiple-Unicast Network Coding and Faster External-Memory Integer Sorting
item.description: arXiv:2610.20079v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In undirected multiple-unicast networks, where independent messages are sent between specified source--destination pairs, network coding allows intermediate nodes to combine messages, whereas fractional routing splits and forwards individual messages along paths without mixing them. Proposed in 2004 by Li and Li and independently by Harvey, Kleinberg, and Lehman, the multiple-unicast conjecture---a central conjecture in network coding with deep connections to computational complexity---asserts that network coding and fractional routing have the same achievable rate region. We construct a counterexample refuting this conjecture and use it to reduce block transfers in external-memory data rearrangement, thereby accelerating external-memory integer sorting and answering in the affirmative the longstanding question of Aggarwal and Vitter (1988) on whether integer operations can beat the comparison-sorting input/output (I/O) bound. Specifically, we give a deterministic sorting algorithm: for $N$ integers of $\Theta(\log N)$ bits, a memory holding $M$ integers, and block transfers of $B$ integers, where $2B\le M\le N$, the number of block transfers is \[ O\!\left(\frac{N}{B}\left[1+ \frac{\log N}{(\log(M/B))^{1-\varepsilon}(\log M)^\varepsilon} \right]\right), \] where $\varepsilon=1.5\times10^{-5}$ is an absolute constant. This bound asymptotically improves on the classical $\Theta\!\left(\frac{N}{B}\left[1+ \frac{\log(N/M)}{\log(M/B)}\right]\right)$ comparison-sorting bound in certain parameter regimes. Under the external-memory model specified in this paper, we have formally verified the algorithm's correctness and I/O complexity bound in Lean~4.
item.dc:creator: Baochun Li, Zongpeng Li, Sirui Liu

item.title: Local Quantum Fault Tolerance Without Expansion
item.description: arXiv:2610.38847v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study fault-tolerant quantum computation using a fixed, local error-correction rule and a geometrically simple code: the cubical $(d,d')$-Toric code with $d',d-d'\geq 2$, including the 4D Toric code. Under sufficiently weak local-stochastic Pauli noise, our construction uses noiseless, bounded-depth classical processing per physical time step. Its correction cycle acts only on the current syndrome, has constant depth, and is repeated unchanged during idle logical computation; it requires neither multiscale decoder states nor scale-dependent communication delays. Our proof treats errors and syndromes as chains in a cubical complex, combining geometric shrinking under the sweep rule with a space--time explanation-tree argument inspired by Toom's theorem. It does not rely on expansion. We establish three results: 1.Explicit higher-dimensional sweep rule. We give a local algorithm for choosing sweep corrections on cubical $(d,d')$-Toric complexes, resolving the local-existence question of Kubica and Preskill. 2. Fault-tolerant computation. We prove a circuit-level threshold theorem for noisy sweep cycles interleaved with logical gates. In particular, the 4D Toric code admits a fixed, constant-depth syndrome-based correction cycle without a multiscale decoder or expansion-based encoding. We do not claim constant total-depth overhead. 3. Ideal decoding under local-stochastic noise. For an initial local-stochastic Pauli error of rate $p$ below threshold, $n^{d+1}$ noiseless sweep cycles recover the encoded state on a side-length-$n$ $(d,d')$-Toric code with probability at least $1-O(\operatorname{poly}(n))p^{\Omega(n)}$, extending earlier guarantees for independent errors.
item.dc:creator: David Ponarovsky

item.title: Efficient Scalable Oversight via Rewinding
item.description: arXiv:2610.40535v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Scalable oversight asks how a weak verifier can check the outputs of computations performed by more powerful AI systems. One proposed approach uses relativizing interactive proofs, in which a weak verifier checks the output of a complex oracle-aided computation by interacting with one or more powerful provers. A prominent example is debate, which is highly efficient but assumes that one of two powerful AI models, or provers, is truthful. For certain classes of oracle-aided computations, this assumption can be removed, but at substantially greater computational cost. In this work, we introduce \emph{rewindable interactive proofs} (RIPs), a new model of relativizing interactive proofs for scalable oversight. In an RIP, the verifier may rewind the prover to an earlier state of the interaction and continue from there. This is possible when the prover is an AI model, since the verifier can save a snapshot of the model's state and later restore it. We construct a relativizing RIP for computations whose outputs are robust to changing a small fraction of oracle answers. Our construction is more efficient than prior relativizing proofs that do not assume a truthful prover, and it uses no cryptography. In our construction the honest prover runs in time linear in that of the original computation, and the verifier, after a one-time preprocessing step, runs in time nearly linear in the input length (which can be much smaller than the computation itself). We implement our protocol, report a preliminary MNIST experiment, and show that an RIP can be faster than a state-of-the-art deployed proof system. RIPs may be of independent interest. Rewinding is possible whenever the verifier controls the prover's machine, for example when the prover runs on trusted hardware or in a virtual machine whose state can be checkpointed.
item.dc:creator: Ziyi Guan, Yael Tauman Kalai, Ron Rothblum, Zoe Xi
